```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse=TRUE,comment="#>")
library(gof)
```

## Start with the sampling design

A successfully fitted model and a finite p-value do not establish that a
residual-process approximation is accurate for a particular design. The
multiplier methods rely on large-sample arguments, independent sampling units
and regular estimation. Counts help describe that situation; they do not
certify it. There is no universal minimum sample size or parameter-to-sample
ratio at which every supported diagnostic becomes calibrated.

Keep the scientific sampling units distinct from the engine's counts. Four
binomial groups with ten independent trials each have four model-data rows
and forty expanded trial units under the binomial model. Correlated trials
within a group would violate that sampling model; expansion does not resolve
the dependence.

```{r grouped}
d <- data.frame(x=0:3,s=c(1,3,6,8),f=c(9,7,4,2))
fit <- glm(cbind(s,f)~x,data=d,family=binomial())
set.seed(62101)
diagnostic <- cumres(fit,variable="x",R=39,plots=0)
diagnostic$design_info
as.data.frame(diagnostic)[,c("variable","test","n","n_rows","n_trials",
                            "estimated_parameters","correction_dimension")]
```

`R=39` keeps this illustration quick; it is not a recommendation for a final
analysis. `subset.max` and the evaluation grid choose where to evaluate a
process, not which observations contribute to estimation or residual sums.
An externally fixed covariate such as `x` supplies a fixed ordering here.
Fitted predictions are estimated orderings and require the additional
conditions and precision policies in the ordering guide.

The multiplier mean diagnostic targets the stated conditional mean with its
adapter's variance/influence assumptions. Response bootstrap instead simulates
an entire binomial or Poisson response law. A response-family assumption is
stronger than specifying a mean alone; a bootstrap result is not a generic
replacement for a mean-model diagnostic.

## What the metadata mean

New objects contain a one-row `design_info` data frame. Summaries retain it;
`as.data.frame()` and optional tidiers repeat its fields on each result row.
The installed `?"cumres-object"` help defines every field.

| Field | Interpretation |
|:--|:--|
| `unit` | Engine unit: row, trial, subject or explicit residual. |
| `n_rows` | Contributing model-data rows before binomial expansion; unknown for arbitrary explicit residual inputs. |
| `n_trials` | Active binomial trials; missing otherwise. |
| `fit_parameters` | Coefficient slots in the source fit, including any aliased slots permitted for specified-null simulation. |
| `estimated_parameters` | Mean/nuisance coefficients adjusted for or refitted by this diagnostic. |
| `fit_design_rank` | Reported lm/glm design rank; missing for other adapters. |
| `correction_dimension` | Dimension of the linear nuisance correction; zero for response bootstrap, which refits instead. |
| `n_components` | Residual components per unit before pooling or aggregation. |

These quantities serve different purposes. Gaussian lm/glm dispersion is not
an lm/glm coefficient slot. An arbitrary callback's correction-vector size
does not establish how many parameters its author estimated. Such an
`estimated_parameters` entry stays missing. SEM data overrides describe the
rows used for the diagnostic, which need not be the original estimation rows.
Objects saved before this metadata existed retain their earlier table columns;
the package does not reconstruct unknown design information from their curves.

For a genuinely specified null, no mean parameters are estimated by the
diagnostic, even if a fitted model supplies its design:

```{r specified}
set.seed(62102)
specified <- cumres_bootstrap(fit,variable="x",null="specified",
                             mean=rep(.5,4),R=39,plots=0)
specified$design_info
```

Here the null probabilities .5 are stipulated independently of these outcomes.
Passing fitted probabilities as `null="specified"` would not make them known.
For fitted-null bootstrap, the mean model is refitted in every simulation.
Neither choice automatically provides good finite-sample calibration.

Precision weights in Gaussian models do not replicate observations. Nor do
ordinal cutpoints or pooled SEM residual coordinates create additional
independent subjects. In particular, `n_components * n` is not an independent
sample-size calculation. See the
[joint, normality and bootstrap guide](joint-normality-bootstrap.html) for
their method-specific constructions.

## Why a small fitted design can matter

An elementary Gaussian calculation illustrates one mechanism; it is not a
general correction formula. With known error variance one, design matrix X,
hat matrix H and M = I - H, fitted residual covariance is M. If A accumulates
observations in a fixed order, a linear corrected process has coefficient
matrix B = A M / sqrt(n). Its sampling covariance is B B'. A multiplier
covariance using the squared fitted residuals has expectation
B diag(diag(M)) B'. Leverage therefore reduces this expected covariance in
this example.

```{r gaussian-mechanism}
X <- cbind(1,0:3)
H <- qr.fitted(qr(X),diag(4))
M <- diag(4)-H
A <- outer(1:4,1:4,">=")*1
B <- A %*% M/sqrt(4)
sampling <- tcrossprod(B)
expected_multiplier <- B %*% diag(diag(M)) %*% t(B)
c(sampling_trace=sum(diag(sampling)),
  multiplier_trace=sum(diag(expected_multiplier)),
  ratio=sum(diag(expected_multiplier))/sum(diag(sampling)))
```

This is an exact covariance identity for this stated linear model, not a
Poisson calibration theorem or a reason to introduce a universal leverage
threshold. Multiplying all Poisson means by ten still leaves the same number
of independently observed rows. Independently replicating the design ten
times changes that number. These are different asymptotic situations.

## Earlier development evidence, with its uncertainty

The package preserves a development screen of two fixed Poisson designs:
200 response cohorts per design and 199 inner simulations per method. The
selected formulas were held fixed, so this screen does not validate a model
selection procedure. It used response-independent lexicographic covariate
cells for ordering. These are earlier results from gof 1.2.1, not a newly
executed qualification study of the current development version.

```{r retained-evidence}
evidence <- system.file("extdata","small-design",package="gof")
screen <- read.csv(file.path(evidence,"development-summary.csv"))
screen
```

The multiplier rejection rates were far from the nominal .05 on these
designs, in both directions. This is a retained limitation, not hidden by a
passing software suite. The response-bootstrap results look more promising
in this screen, but 200 cohorts give wide uncertainty. An interval containing
.05 is not evidence of equivalence to .05 or a qualification pass.

`rejection.lower` counts only definite rejections; `rejection.upper` also
counts decisions left unresolved. Their denominator includes every planned
cohort. `mc.lower` and `mc.upper` form a pointwise 95% Clopper--Pearson
envelope using those lower and upper rejection counts. They are not
simultaneous intervals across all rows. They describe outer simulation
uncertainty at the stated inner simulation budget, not the infinite-budget
tail probability. `development-records.csv` retains all 1,600
method/statistic records; `PROVENANCE.json` and `README.md` explain their
origin and the accompanying response-free design objects.

Fresh statistical qualification remains deferred behind independent review.
No recommendation to switch methods automatically follows from this screen.

## Read availability and failures before interpreting tails

* `informative=FALSE` identifies a structurally recognized lack of information
  and yields p-values of one. That is not affirmative model evidence. Some
  custom ordinal aggregations have a constant, nonzero descriptive curve even
  though their score-space variation is zero.
* `informative=NA` can mean unavailable metadata or numerical indeterminacy.
  Missing metadata alone does not withhold an otherwise available p-value;
  diagnosed indeterminacy does. Read the adapter's status and warnings.
* Unresolved fitted ordering withholds inferential tails under the default
  policy. A joint family with an unresolved member is not silently reduced to
  the remaining members. See [ordering and ties](ordering-and-ties.html).
* Bootstrap refit failures retain their place in the denominator. Affected
  point estimates are missing and `p.lower`/`p.upper` bound the possible
  completed simulation tail. These completion bounds are not confidence
  intervals. Analytic zero/one boundary cases have their documented special
  handling; they do not establish general finite-sample validity.
* Unsupported or invalid model constructions may raise an error. In a batch
  assessment, retain and report those errors separately. Dropping them with
  `na.rm=TRUE`, or replacing them with p-values zero or one, changes the
  question being assessed.

Choose the diagnostic, ordering family, measurement resolution, windows and
simulation budget before inspecting the diagnostic outcomes. Increasing R
reduces inner Monte Carlo uncertainty; it does not repair a model assumption
or a poorly calibrated approximation. Report simulation uncertainty and
failures alongside conclusions. For approximate SEM normality, retain its
Gaussian, independent-subject and regularity assumptions and its documented
first-order nuisance correction.

  cumulative residuals. *Biometrics*, 58, 1--12.

* R Core Team. [Generalized linear models](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/glm.html):

* R Core Team. [Exact binomial test](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/binom.test.html):
